title: Neutralisation of acids and salt production

notes.definition: Acids are neutralised by alkalis (soluble metal hydroxides) and bases (insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides) to produce a salt and water, and by metal carbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide. The salt made depends on the acid used and on the positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate.
explanation: A base is a substance that neutralises an acid to form a salt and water. Metal oxides and metal hydroxides are bases. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, such as sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide or calcium hydroxide. So all alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis: copper oxide and copper hydroxide are bases that do not dissolve in water. The general equations are acid + alkali → salt + water and acid + base → salt + water. For example: NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) and CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l).

Metal carbonates also neutralise acids, but they produce carbon dioxide as well: acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. You see fizzing as the gas is given off, and the gas turns limewater milky. For example: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). If the reaction is done in an open flask on a balance, the mass goes down because the carbon dioxide escapes into the air.

The name of a salt has two parts. The first part comes from the positive (metal) ion in the base, alkali or carbonate. The second part comes from the acid: hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates and sulfuric acid produces sulfates. So potassium hydroxide and nitric acid make potassium nitrate, and zinc oxide and sulfuric acid make zinc sulfate. To make a particular salt, choose the acid that gives the right negative ion and a base, alkali or carbonate that contains the right metal.

You can work out the formula of a salt from the charges on its ions, because the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge. Useful negative ions: chloride Cl⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, oxide O²⁻ and carbonate CO₃²⁻. Sodium chloride is NaCl (1+ and 1−). Magnesium sulfate is MgSO₄ (2+ and 2−). Calcium nitrate needs two nitrate ions to balance Ca²⁺, so it is Ca(NO₃)₂: brackets show that the whole NO₃ group is doubled. Aluminium sulfate needs two Al³⁺ (6+) and three SO₄²⁻ (6−), giving Al₂(SO₄)₃.

Once you know the formulae you can write balanced equations. Balance the metal and the acid's negative ion first, then the hydrogen and oxygen by adjusting water. For sulfuric acid with sodium hydroxide: 2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l). For magnesium oxide with nitric acid: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). For sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acid: Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
keyFacts: Acid + base (metal oxide or insoluble metal hydroxide) → salt + water.
Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
An alkali is a soluble base, for example sodium hydroxide; bases include metal oxides and insoluble metal hydroxides.
Hydrochloric acid → chlorides; nitric acid → nitrates; sulfuric acid → sulfates.
The first part of the salt name comes from the metal ion in the base, alkali or carbonate.
Formulae of acids: HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄.
Ion formulae: Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻, O²⁻, CO₃²⁻.
In a salt formula the positive and negative charges balance, for example Ca(NO₃)₂ and Al₂(SO₄)₃.

keyTerms.definition: A reaction in which an acid reacts with a base, alkali or carbonate, so that the solution is no longer acidic.
A substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water, such as a metal oxide or metal hydroxide.
A base that dissolves in water, such as sodium hydroxide; its solution contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻.
An ionic compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal (or ammonium) ion.
A compound containing a metal ion and the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, such as calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.
A salt made from nitric acid, containing NO₃⁻ ions.
A salt made from sulfuric acid, containing SO₄²⁻ ions.
A salt made from hydrochloric acid, containing Cl⁻ ions.

workedExamples.title: Predicting the products
workedExamples.question: Name the products when (a) potassium hydroxide reacts with nitric acid, (b) copper carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid.
steps: (a) An alkali + acid gives a salt + water. The metal is potassium and nitric acid gives nitrates.
So the products are potassium nitrate and water.
(b) A carbonate + acid gives a salt + water + carbon dioxide. The metal is copper and sulfuric acid gives sulfates.
So the products are copper sulfate, water and carbon dioxide.
workedExamples.answer: (a) potassium nitrate + water; (b) copper sulfate + water + carbon dioxide

workedExamples.title: Working out the formula of a salt
workedExamples.question: Work out the formula of (a) calcium nitrate and (b) aluminium sulfate.
steps: (a) Ions: Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻. Two NO₃⁻ ions (2−) balance one Ca²⁺ (2+).
Use brackets to show two nitrate groups: Ca(NO₃)₂.
(b) Ions: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻. The lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6.
Two Al³⁺ give 6+; three SO₄²⁻ give 6−. Formula: Al₂(SO₄)₃.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'base' and 'alkali' mean exactly the same thing.
misconceptions.right: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Copper oxide is a base but not an alkali because it is insoluble.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all neutralisation reactions produce carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.right: Only carbonates produce carbon dioxide. Acids with alkalis or bases produce just a salt and water.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the salt is always sodium chloride.
misconceptions.right: 'Salt' is a general name for any ionic compound made from an acid, such as copper sulfate or potassium nitrate. Sodium chloride is just one example.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write calcium nitrate as CaNO₃₂ or CaNO₃.
misconceptions.right: Two nitrate ions are needed to balance Ca²⁺, and the whole group is doubled using brackets: Ca(NO₃)₂.

realWorld: Farmers spread lime (calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide or calcium carbonate) on acidic soils to neutralise them.
Indigestion tablets contain bases or carbonates, such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate, to neutralise excess stomach acid.
Fertilisers such as potassium nitrate are salts made by neutralisation reactions.
Acidic waste from factories is neutralised with bases before it is released into rivers.
examTips: Learn the three patterns: acid + alkali → salt + water; acid + base → salt + water; acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
For the salt name, take the metal from the base/alkali/carbonate and the ending from the acid: chloride, nitrate or sulfate.
Balance charges to get formulae, and use brackets for groups like NO₃, SO₄, OH and CO₃ when there is more than one.
Balance equations by placing numbers in front of formulae only. Never change a formula to make it balance.
If asked what you would see with a carbonate, say 'fizzing' or 'bubbles'; the test for carbon dioxide is that limewater turns milky (cloudy).
summary: Alkalis are soluble bases; bases include metal oxides and insoluble hydroxides.
Acid + alkali or base → salt + water.
Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Hydrochloric acid → chlorides, nitric acid → nitrates, sulfuric acid → sulfates.
The metal in the salt comes from the base, alkali or carbonate.
Use ion charges to deduce salt formulae, such as Ca(NO₃)₂ and Al₂(SO₄)₃.

options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Acid + alkali → salt + water. Hydrogen forms with metals and carbon dioxide forms with carbonates.

questions.question: What are the products when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
A salt, hydrogen and carbon dioxide
markScheme: 1 mark: a salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbonates give carbon dioxide as well as a salt and water. Hydrogen is not produced.

questions.question: Which salt is produced when sodium hydroxide reacts with nitric acid?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid produces nitrates. Chlorides come from hydrochloric acid and sulfates from sulfuric acid.

questions.question: Which substance is a base but not an alkali?
questions.explanation: Copper oxide neutralises acids but does not dissolve in water, so it is a base that is not an alkali. The three hydroxides are soluble, so they are alkalis.

markScheme: 1 mark: zinc oxide and hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Zinc must come from the base and chloride from hydrochloric acid. Sulfuric acid would give zinc sulfate and nitric acid would give zinc nitrate.

questions.question:

What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
questions.explanation: Two nitrate ions are needed to balance the 2+ charge on calcium. Brackets show that the whole NO₃ group is doubled.

questions.question: Aluminium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid. What is the formula of the salt produced?
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻: two Al³⁺ (6+) balance three SO₄²⁻ (6−). Al₃(SO₄)₂ has the numbers swapped, giving 9+ and 4−.

questions.question: Which is the correctly balanced equation for calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Calcium chloride is CaCl₂, so 2HCl are needed. The two H atoms go into one H₂O. Hydrogen gas is not a product of acid and carbonate.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Ca = 40; N = 14; O = 16
questions.explanation: The bracket means everything inside is multiplied by 2: 2 N and 6 O. 40 + (2 × 14) + (6 × 16) = 40 + 28 + 96 = 164.

questions.question:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of potassium sulfate, K₂SO₄.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): K = 39; S = 32; O = 16
questions.explanation: Two potassium atoms: 2 × 39 = 78. Sulfate: 32 + (4 × 16) = 96. Total 78 + 96 = 174.

Magnesium oxide reacts with dilute nitric acid.
Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.

questions.explanation: Magnesium nitrate is Mg(NO₃)₂, so 2HNO₃ are needed. The 2 H atoms and the O from the oxide make one H₂O.

questions.question:
Dilute hydrochloric acid is reacted separately with:
• sodium hydroxide solution
• copper oxide powder
• calcium carbonate.
Compare the three reactions.
In your answer you should include:
• the type of substance reacting with the acid
• the products and a word equation for each reaction
• what you would observe.
markScheme: Indicative content: sodium hydroxide is an alkali (soluble base): sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water; no visible change (colourless solution stays colourless) but the mixture warms; copper oxide is a base (insoluble metal oxide): copper oxide + hydrochloric acid → copper chloride + water; black solid disappears and solution turns blue-green; calcium carbonate is a metal carbonate: calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide; fizzing, solid disappears, gas turns limewater milky; all three are neutralisation reactions producing a chloride salt and water; only the carbonate gives carbon dioxide.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three reactions correctly described with products, word equations and observations, and a clear comparison (similarities and the difference with the carbonate).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two reactions correctly described with products and some observations or comparison.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about products, such as a salt is made, with limited detail.
questions.explanation: All three neutralise the acid and make chlorides. Alkalis and bases give salt + water; carbonates also give carbon dioxide, which is why they fizz.

questions.question:
A student has two unlabelled white powders.
One powder is magnesium oxide and the other is magnesium carbonate.
Describe how the student could use dilute hydrochloric acid to identify each powder.
Explain the results.
markScheme: Indicative content: add a small spatula of each powder to separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid; magnesium carbonate fizzes (gives off a gas) but magnesium oxide does not fizz; bubble the gas through limewater, which turns milky, confirming carbon dioxide; carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide (magnesium chloride + water + carbon dioxide); oxide + acid → salt + water only (magnesium chloride + water); both powders dissolve to give colourless solutions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear method, correct observations for both powders and explanation linked to carbon dioxide being produced only by the carbonate.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that one fizzes or that carbonates give carbon dioxide, with little method or explanation.
questions.explanation: Both are neutralised by acid, but only the carbonate releases carbon dioxide, so fizzing (and a positive limewater test) identifies it.

questions.question:
Predict the products of each reaction.
Write a balanced symbol equation for each reaction.
(a) lithium hydroxide, LiOH, and nitric acid
(b) zinc carbonate, ZnCO₃, and sulfuric acid
markScheme: Indicative content: (a) lithium nitrate and water; LiOH + HNO₃ → LiNO₃ + H₂O; (b) zinc sulfate, water and carbon dioxide; ZnCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂; state symbols may be included: (aq), (aq), (aq), (l) for (a) and (s), (aq), (aq), (l), (g) for (b).
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct products and correctly balanced equations for both reactions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct products for one or both reactions, with equations missing or incorrect.
questions.explanation: Li⁺ and NO₃⁻ give LiNO₃; Zn²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give ZnSO₄. Both equations balance with one of each reactant.

questions.question: Which of these substances is an alkali?
questions.explanation: Potassium hydroxide is a soluble metal hydroxide, so it is an alkali. Copper hydroxide and iron oxide are insoluble bases, and calcium carbonate is a carbonate.
